title: Method of Reasoning
summary: Describe how the argument works, not what it says. Map the moves in plain words, then match each part of the abstract choice to the text.

slides.title: How, not what
body: Method questions ask you to describe the argument’s technique: using an analogy, citing a counterexample, eliminating alternatives, pointing out an inconsistency.
The choices are abstract. Translate each one back into the specifics of the argument. If any part doesn’t match, the choice is out.

slides.title: How you’ll see it
stems: Which one of the following most accurately describes the technique of reasoning used in the argument?
The speaker responds to the other by…
The argument employs which one of the following reasoning techniques?

steps.label: Map in plain words
steps.do: “She takes his claim, finds three similar cases where it failed, and says it will fail here too.”

steps.label: Name the move
steps.do: Counterexample, analogy, similar cases, elimination, attacking a premise, showing a consequence is absurd.

steps.label: Translate the choices
steps.do: For each part of a choice, point to the sentence it describes.

steps.label: Kill on one mismatch
steps.do: A choice with one part that didn’t happen is wrong, however good the rest is.

slides.title: Level 1: one case against a general rule
slides.stimulus: Ravi: Every restaurant that stays successful for years has a famous chef. That is what keeps the crowds coming. Mina: That cannot be right. Harper's Diner has been packed every night for ten years, and its cook is unknown outside the neighborhood.
slides.stem: Mina responds to Ravi's claim by

choices.A: questioning Ravi's reasons for making the claim
choices.B: showing that Ravi's claim, taken seriously, would have an absurd result
choices.C: pointing out that Ravi has offered no evidence for the claim
choices.D: drawing an analogy between restaurants and some other kind of business
choices.E: citing a specific case that conflicts with Ravi's general claim

steps.label: Ravi's claim
steps.note: A general rule: lasting restaurants all have famous chefs.
steps.highlight: Every restaurant that stays successful for years has a famous chef

steps.label: Mina's move
steps.note: She names one restaurant. It has lasted and its cook is unknown.
steps.highlight: Harper's Diner has been packed every night for ten years

steps.label: Name the move
steps.note: One case that breaks a general rule is a counterexample.

steps.label: Translate the choices
steps.note: In E, 'specific case' is Harper's Diner and 'general claim' is Ravi's rule. Every part matches.

why.A: Mina never mentions Ravi's motives or reasons for speaking.
why.B: Mina does not follow Ravi's claim to an absurd result. She gives a real case against it.
why.C: Ravi did give a reason, and Mina does not complain about missing evidence. She offers evidence of her own.
why.D: No other type of business appears in the exchange, so there is no analogy.
why.E: Correct. Harper's Diner is a specific case that conflicts with Ravi's general rule.

slides.title: Level 2: the method, step by step
slides.stimulus: Mayor Duval says the new stadium will pay for itself through increased tax revenue. But the three most recent stadiums built in comparable cities all generated far less tax revenue than their supporters predicted. There is little reason to expect Duval's stadium to do better.

choices.A: showing that the mayor has a personal interest in the stadium being built
choices.B: using the outcomes of similar cases to cast doubt on a prediction
choices.C: arguing that a claim is false because no evidence has been offered for it
choices.D: pointing out an inconsistency in the mayor's own statements
choices.E: questioning the accuracy of the mayor's figures about current tax revenue

steps.label: The claim attacked
steps.note: Duval predicts the stadium will pay for itself.
steps.highlight: the new stadium will pay for itself through increased tax revenue

steps.label: The support
steps.note: Three similar stadiums fell short of predictions.
steps.highlight: the three most recent stadiums built in comparable cities

steps.label: Name the move
steps.note: Comparable cases are used to doubt a prediction.

why.A: The mayor's motives are never mentioned.
why.B: Correct. Similar cases (comparable stadiums) cast doubt on the prediction.
why.C: The argument offers evidence against the claim; it doesn't rely on a lack of evidence.
why.D: Only one statement by the mayor is cited, so there's no inconsistency.
why.E: The mayor gave no current figures; the argument is about future revenue.

slides.title: Level 3: elimination, with a tempting look-alike
slides.stimulus: Lena: The office coffee machine stopped working sometime between Friday evening and Monday morning. Only three explanations are plausible: the cleaning crew damaged it, a power surge fried it, or it simply wore out. It was working at five o'clock on Friday. The building's security log shows that the crew did not enter at any point that weekend. And the other equipment on the same circuit is running normally, which it would not be after a surge. So the machine must have worn out.

choices.A: rejecting two of three possible explanations on the basis of specific evidence, and then accepting the remaining one
choices.B: inferring that one event caused another from the fact that the second followed the first
choices.C: dismissing two of the three possible explanations because no one has yet found any direct evidence in their favor
choices.D: showing that two of the three possible explanations are inconsistent with each other and so cannot both be true
choices.E: applying a general rule about how office equipment fails to the case of one particular machine

steps.label: Map the claim
steps.note: A machine broke. Three explanations are on the table, and the third is the one Lena accepts.
steps.highlight: the cleaning crew damaged it, a power surge fried it, or it simply wore out

steps.label: Track each explanation
steps.note: Crew: the log says it never came in. Surge: nearby equipment is fine. Each is ruled out by a specific fact.
steps.highlight: the other equipment on the same circuit is running normally

steps.label: Name the move
steps.note: Ruling out alternatives one by one and keeping what is left is elimination.

steps.label: Test the near traps
steps.note: C sounds close, but Lena rules explanations out with evidence against them, not with a lack of evidence for them. B fails too: the timing only sets the window and is not offered as proof of cause.

steps.label: Confirm
steps.note: A matches every part: two rejected, on specific evidence, and the third accepted.

why.A: Correct. The crew and the surge are each rejected on specific evidence, and wearing out is accepted as what remains.
why.B: The weekend timing only sets the window for the failure. Lena does not argue that something caused the failure because it came just before it.
why.C: Tempting, but Lena has evidence against each explanation (the log, the working equipment). She does not dismiss them for lacking support.
why.D: Lena never compares the explanations with each other. She tests each one against the facts.
why.E: No general rule about equipment is stated or applied.

slides.title: Level 4: granting the evidence while taking away its force
slides.stimulus: Maya: Of the cities that installed speed cameras last decade, nearly all saw traffic deaths fall in the following years. Clearly, speed cameras save lives. Jon: Look at when cities install them. They usually do so right after an unusually deadly stretch of accidents, and any unusually bad stretch tends to be followed by a milder one no matter what is done. A fall in deaths is exactly what we would see in those cities even if the cameras did nothing at all. I'm not saying the cameras are useless, only that your figures do not show that they work.
slides.stem: Jon responds to Maya's argument by

choices.A: disputing the accuracy of the figures Maya cites
choices.B: granting Maya's figures but showing that they are inconsistent with her conclusion
choices.C: granting Maya's figures but giving a reason to expect them even if her conclusion were false
choices.D: citing a parallel case in which the same reasoning leads to a conclusion that is plainly false
choices.E: granting Maya's figures but arguing that they support a conclusion opposite to hers

steps.label: Maya's claim
steps.note: Deaths fell in camera cities, so cameras save lives.

steps.label: Does Jon grant the figures?
steps.note: Yes. He never questions the drop. He says it is what we would expect anyway.
steps.highlight: exactly what we would see in those cities even if the cameras did nothing at all

steps.label: Find his reason
steps.note: Cities install cameras after a bad stretch, and bad stretches tend to ease on their own.
steps.highlight: any unusually bad stretch tends to be followed by a milder one no matter what is done

steps.label: Name the move
steps.note: He shows the evidence would appear whether or not the conclusion were true. So it does not support the conclusion. He does not claim the conclusion is false.

steps.label: Kill the near twins
steps.note: B says 'inconsistent', but Jon says the figures fit cameras doing nothing, not that they clash with Maya's view. E says 'opposite', but Jon says he is not calling the cameras useless.

why.A: Jon accepts the figures. He only argues about what they show.
why.B: Close, but 'inconsistent' is wrong. Jon says the figures are expected even if cameras do nothing. He does not say they conflict with Maya's conclusion.
why.C: Correct. He grants the drop and gives a reason to expect it without any effect from cameras.
why.D: Jon cites no parallel case. His reason is about when cities install cameras.
why.E: Jon states he is not saying the cameras are useless, so he does not argue for the opposite conclusion.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Describe the moves in plain words first.
Common moves: counterexample, analogy, similar cases, elimination, absurd consequence.
Every part of the right choice maps to the text.
One part that didn’t happen sinks a choice.
